title: Trump: The Obama administration cuts funding for Soviet Union research
description_short: Trump: The Obama administration cuts funding for Soviet Union research
description_medium: Trump File dates the Obama administration’s reduction in funding for research on the former Soviet Union to October 2014 and says it continued into 2015 as resources shifted to Syria, ISIS, and gun violence. The linked timeline gives no budget amounts, programs, or decision records. The event predates Trump and the supplied material does not explain its relevance to this collection.
description_long: The linked Trump File timeline dates the Obama administration’s reduction in funding for research on the former Soviet Union to October 2014 and says the shift continued into 2015. It attributes the change to resources being redirected toward Syria, ISIS, and gun violence. The page does not identify a budget line, the amount of funding reduced, the agencies or research programs affected, or the documents behind the stated reason. This entry predates Donald Trump’s presidency and the supplied material does not establish a meaningful connection between the budget decision and Trump. The event can be described as an Obama administration funding change, but its scale and effect cannot be assessed from the linked page alone. More importantly for this collection, the record’s “Trump:” framing is unexplained. A budget document or agency record could establish the programs and amounts involved; a separate source would be needed to show why the decision belongs among Trump-related events. Until that connection is supplied, the item remains unresolved rather than a completed Trump entry.

title: Trump purges 46 attorneys from the DOJ, including one asked to investigate him
description_short: Trump purges 46 attorneys from the DOJ, including one asked to investigate him
description_medium: On March 10, 2017, Trump and Attorney General Jeff Sessions asked 46 U.S. attorneys appointed under Barack Obama to resign. Trump File’s account says the mass request was unusual and notes that Manhattan U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara had been urged by government watchdogs to examine possible foreign-government payments to Trump. Bharara was among those asked to leave.
description_long: A Trump File timeline entry dated March 10, 2017, says President Donald Trump and Attorney General Jeff Sessions sought the immediate resignations of 46 U.S. attorneys appointed during the Obama administration. The page distinguishes the broad request from the routine practice of presidents appointing their own prosecutors, describing the number and lack of advance notice as unusual. It identifies Preet Bharara, the U.S. attorney for Manhattan, as one of those asked to leave. The entry links this episode to a letter from government watchdogs urging Bharara to examine whether Trump had violated the Constitution’s emoluments clause by accepting payments from foreign governments. It also notes that the calls came after commentator Sean Hannity publicly urged Trump to purge Obama-era officials. The cited reporting establishes timing and context, but does not show that Bharara was removed because of a particular investigation. The mass resignations therefore raise an oversight concern without, by themselves, proving a retaliatory motive.

preserved_fields.title: Trump purges 46 attorneys from the DOJ, including one asked to investigate him
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump purges 46 attorneys from the DOJ, including one asked to investigate him

notes: Completed from the linked timeline’s account and its reproduced New York Times context. The description distinguishes the mass resignation request from the unproven claim that Bharara was removed to stop an investigation.

General contractor Irving Fischer testified that union representatives threatened a switchboard operator with a knife while pressing for no-show jobs. The reporting says Trump paid inflated concrete prices and received “union peace”; it does not say Trump directed the threat.

The union violence extended to Trump's relationship with Teamsters official John Cody who controlled concrete truck flow and was convicted of racketeering, with Trump providing free apartments and financial arrangements to Cody's associates while benefiting from union compliance achieved through organized crime intimidation and violence. The construction violence created dangerous working conditions where union members faced physical threats and criminal intimidation designed to ensure Trump's projects proceeded without labor disruption while workers lost bargaining power and safety protections through systematic organized crime control. The union intimidation established Trump's systematic approach to labor relations and worker rights, demonstrating willingness to benefit from organized crime violence while participating in criminal enterprises that suppressed worker protections through systematic intimidation and physical threats that prioritized construction profits over worker safety and legitimate labor rights.

title: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer
description_short: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer
description_medium: On January 16, 2021, Acting Defense Secretary Christopher Miller ordered the National Security Agency to install Michael Ellis as its top lawyer. Trump File says the NSA installed Ellis the next day and that he started on January 19. Ellis had been a lawyer for Representative Devin Nunes and was linked to the Trump–Ukraine controversy.
description_long: A Trump File timeline entry dated January 16, 2021, reports that Acting Defense Secretary Christopher Miller ordered the National Security Agency to install Michael Ellis as the agency’s top lawyer. Ellis had previously worked for Representative Devin Nunes and was associated with the controversy over Trump’s pressure on Ukraine. The timeline says the NSA carried out the order the following day and that Ellis’s first day in the role was January 19. The account describes a late-term personnel decision made by an acting defense secretary, rather than an order personally signed by Trump. It places the appointment in the final days of the administration, when Ellis’s installation was contested. The linked Washington Post report supplies additional reporting on Miller’s direction to the NSA director, while the assignment’s synopsis provides the dates of installation and Ellis’s first day. The record documents an agency leadership appointment and its timing; it does not establish that Ellis’s prior work meant he would act improperly as NSA general counsel.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer

notes: Completed from the linked Trump File timeline and Washington Post report. The description attributes the installation order to Acting Defense Secretary Christopher Miller rather than to Trump personally.

title: Trump: REPORT: Trump demands fealty from national-security hires
description_short: Trump: REPORT: Trump demands fealty from national-security hires
description_medium: Trump File quotes a Washington Post report that two former officials considered for intelligence-community posts were asked whether January 6 was “an inside job” and whether the 2020 election was “stolen.” The account says applicants were rejected if they did not answer as Trump wanted. It is based on anonymous sources and does not establish that every national-security applicant received the questions.
description_long: The linked Trump File page reproduces a Washington Post account by Ellen Nakashima and Warren P. Strobel about screening for intelligence and law-enforcement positions. It says two former officials being considered for intelligence-community jobs were asked to answer yes or no to whether January 6 was “an inside job” and whether the 2020 election was “stolen.” The people interviewed by the Post spoke anonymously, and the page says applicants were rejected if they did not answer as Trump wanted. The report describes a loyalty test tied to false claims about the election and the attack on the Capitol. That practice, if accurately reported, raises concerns about whether applicants’ political agreement was being weighed over candor and professional judgment in national-security roles. The material concerns several candidates and does not establish that every FBI or CIA applicant faced the questions, who administered them, or the full number of people screened. The account is attributed to the reporting reproduced on Trump File, rather than treated as a formal written hiring policy.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: REPORT: Trump demands fealty from national-security hires
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: REPORT: Trump demands fealty from national-security hires

notes: Completed after a focused read of the linked Trump File page, which reproduces the specific questions and applicant context attributed to the Washington Post. The description retains the anonymous-source caveat and limits the claim to reported candidates.

title: Trump: LEAK: Elon Musk's DOGE infiltrates National Institutes of Health
description_short: Trump: LEAK: Elon Musk's DOGE infiltrates National Institutes of Health
description_medium: A Trump File timeline summarizing WIRED reporting says four DOGE-associated employees had NIH email addresses, and three worked in the department controlling the agency’s central electronic business system. The system included finance, budget, procurement, property management, and grant tracking. The source reports access to sensitive financial systems but does not identify particular transactions or records viewed.
description_long: The linked Trump File timeline, dated February 24, 2025, summarizes WIRED’s review of internal documents and government records concerning Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. It names Luke Farritor, Rachel Riley, Jeremy Lewin, and Clark Minor as DOGE-associated people with NIH email addresses. The page says three worked in the department overseeing NIH’s central electronic business system, which includes finance, budgeting, procurement, property management, and grant tracking. It reports that the operatives gained access to sensitive financial systems. The account describes the employees’ institutional access, not specific transactions they made or particular personal or grant records they viewed. It also notes that Farritor had an email address associated with the General Services Administration. These details raise questions about access controls and oversight when employees associated with a government-efficiency initiative work inside a research agency’s financial systems. The source does not establish that the employees misused data or changed NIH spending decisions. The claims remain attributed to the internal documents and records reviewed by WIRED, as summarized by the linked timeline.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: LEAK: Elon Musk's DOGE infiltrates National Institutes of Health

title: Trump and Qatar bolster ties after jet bribe
description_short: Trump and Qatar bolster ties after jet bribe
description_medium: During Trump’s May 14, 2025, visit to Qatar, Qatar Airways announced plans to buy 210 Boeing aircraft and the two governments announced defense agreements. The Trump File timeline also discusses Qatar’s $400 million aircraft gift to the United States for possible use as Air Force One. The page raises conflict-of-interest concerns but does not establish a quid pro quo.
description_long: The linked Trump File timeline describes Donald Trump’s May 14, 2025, visit to Qatar alongside economic and defense announcements. Qatar Airways said it intended to purchase 210 Boeing aircraft, while the United States and Qatar announced defense cooperation that included potential sales of counter-drone and remotely piloted aircraft systems. The timeline also notes Qatar’s offer of a Boeing 747-8, valued there at about $400 million, for possible use as Air Force One. These developments prompted conflict-of-interest questions because the aircraft offer came from a foreign government while Trump was president and business ties between Qatar and Trump associates were also reported. The entry’s original use of “bribe” states a conclusion about motive that the linked account does not establish as a legal finding or proven exchange. The known facts are the visit, the announced order and defense agreements, and the reported aircraft gift. A specific quid pro quo would require evidence connecting the gift to the commercial or defense announcements.

preserved_fields.title: Trump and Qatar bolster ties after jet bribe
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump and Qatar bolster ties after jet bribe

notes: Completed with a factual title and descriptions of the visit, announcements, and aircraft gift. The original “bribe” label was narrowed because the linked account does not establish a quid pro quo.

title: Trump allows Hegseth aide to bypass law
description_short: Trump allows Hegseth aide to bypass law
description_medium: A Trump File report says Marine Colonel Ricky D. Buria received an exception to retire at his current rank after holding the rank for less than three years. The page says he served as a senior adviser to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. It also reports that Trump said he did not know who Buria was and would review the matter, which conflicts with the original title’s claim that Trump allowed the exception.
description_long: The linked Trump File account, dated July 21, 2025, says Marine Colonel Ricky D. Buria received an exception to retire at his current rank after holding the rank for less than the three years the page says are generally required. It describes Buria as an adviser to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and says Hegseth had made him a senior adviser while he was still in the Marines. The account also reports that Trump said he had “no idea” who Buria was and would look into the matter, adding that he would recommend against the exception if the reporting were true. That statement does not support the original headline’s assertion that Trump personally allowed Buria to bypass the rule. The record is more accurately framed as a reported retirement exception involving a Hegseth adviser, with Trump’s public response included as context. The source says an exception may be granted for extreme hardship or exceptional circumstances but reports no evidence that Buria met those criteria.

preserved_fields.title: Trump allows Hegseth aide to bypass law
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump allows Hegseth aide to bypass law

notes: Completed with a title correction because the linked account says Trump denied knowing Buria and promised to review the matter, rather than authorizing the exception.

title: Trump admin offers military funeral honors to criminal Ashli Babbitt
description_short: Trump admin offers military funeral honors to criminal Ashli Babbitt
description_medium: The Trump File timeline says the U.S. government offered military funeral honors for Ashli Babbitt on August 29, 2025, and invited her family to the Pentagon. It reports that Judicial Watch had requested the honors and quotes an Air Force spokesperson saying they were offered after a review. The source does not establish the original title’s “criminal” label as a court finding.
description_long: A Trump File timeline entry dated August 29, 2025, reports that the U.S. government offered military funeral honors for Ashli Babbitt and invited her family to the Pentagon. It says Judicial Watch had a role in requesting the honors and quotes an Air Force spokesperson stating that the offer followed a review of the circumstances. The page also notes that the Trump administration had paid about $5 million to settle the family’s wrongful-death lawsuit. Babbitt was shot and killed by Capitol police during the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. The source’s original headline calls her a “criminal,” but the supplied account does not identify a criminal conviction; the label is therefore removed from the corrected title and not presented as a legal finding here. The reported event is the government’s offer of honors, not evidence that a ceremony took place or that the offer represented a formal change in military policy.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump admin offers military funeral honors to criminal Ashli Babbitt

title: ICE Gains Access to Biometric Iris-Recognition Tools for Mobile Devices
description_short: ICE Gains Access to Biometric Iris-Recognition Tools for Mobile Devices
description_medium: The supplied account says ICE gained access in late September 2025 to Bi2 Technologies’ IRIS and MORIS systems, which use iris biometrics for identification through a mobile device. The company described the systems’ identification capabilities. The packet does not establish whether ICE purchased, licensed, tested or operationally deployed them, or whether anyone was scanned.
description_long: The supplied account says Immigration and Customs Enforcement gained access in late September 2025 to two Bi2 Technologies systems: the Inmate Identification Recognition System, or IRIS, and the Mobile Offender Recognition and Information System, or MORIS. It describes IRIS as a real-time iris-biometric network and says MORIS can run on Apple, Android and Microsoft devices, allowing an agent to collect biometric information with a mobile camera. Bi2 Technologies claims its system can identify people quickly from a distance. The linked material does not clarify whether ICE purchased, licensed or tested the tools, or whether agents used them operationally. It does not identify the encounters or groups in which scans could occur, how consent would work, what data would be retained, who could access records or how false matches would be handled. Access to a biometric system is not the same as documented deployment or proof that a particular person was scanned. The entry supports a report that ICE obtained access to iris-recognition tools, while the scope, safeguards and real-world use remain unknown.
notes: Completed after the linked timeline confirmed ICE’s reported access to Bi2 Technologies’ IRIS and MORIS systems. Existing descriptions accurately distinguish access and technical capability from documented scans or operational use.
